### Exercise 1 {-}

Create a vector of three elements (2,4,6) and name that vector `vec_a`. Create a second vector, `vec_b`, that contains $(8,10,12)$. Add these two vectors together and name the result `vec_c`.

```{r}
vec_a <- c(2,4,6)
vec_b <- c(8,10,12)

(vec_c <- vec_a + vec_b)
```
I created vec_a and vec_b, then added them together to get vec_c using the c() function.

### Exercise 2 {-}

Create a vector, named `vec_d`, that contains only two elements (14,20). Add this vector to `vec_a`. What is the result and what do you think R did (look up the recycling rule using Google)? What is the warning message that R gives you?

```{r}
vec_d <- c(14,20)

vec_a + vec_d
```
The given warning is saying that in R "recycled" the shorter vector (vecd) in order to match the longer vector (veca). The warning given above is saying that the longer vector (3 elements) is not a multiple of the shorter vector (2 elements)

### Exercise 3 {-}

Next add $5$ to the vector `vec_a`. What is the result and what did R do? Why doesn't in give you a warning message similar to what you saw in the previous problem?

```{r}
vec_a + 5
```
It added 5 to every element in the vector, vec_a. It did not give a warning message because 5 is 1) not a vector and 2) it is a multiple of 3 and thus be added to every element in vec_a.

### Exercise 6 {-}

Generate a vector of $21$ elements that are evenly placed between $0$ and $1$ using the `seq()` command and name this vector `x`. 

```{r}
(x <- seq(from = 0, to = 1, length.out = 21)) # can't have a by if using length.out, from and by
```
21 elements evenly placed between 0 and 1 are arranged in increments of .05.

### Exercise 11 {-}

Create and manipulate a data frame.

**a)** Create a `data.frame` named `my.trees` that has the following columns:

  + Girth = {8.3, 8.6, 8.8, 10.5, 10.7, 10.8, 11.0}
  + Height= {70, 65, 63, 72, 81, 83, 66}
  + Volume= {10.3, 10.3, 10.2, 16.4, 18.8, 19.7, 15.6}
  
```{r}
my.trees <- data.frame(
  Girth = c(8.3, 8.6, 8.8, 10.5, 10.7, 10.8, 11.0), 
  Height= c(70, 65, 63, 72, 81, 83, 66),
  Volume= c(10.3, 10.3, 10.2, 16.4, 18.8, 19.7, 15.6)
)
```

I created a dataframe. 

Complete the following without using `dplyr` functions

**b)** Extract the third observation (i.e. the third row)
```{r}
my.trees[3,] #using a position
```
I used bracket notation to extract the 3rd row. 

**c)** Extract the Girth column referring to it by name (don't use a numerical value based on column position).

```{r}
my.trees[,'Girth'] #Using the column name but brackets to accurately call the desired column 
```
I used bracket notation to extract the Girth column from my my.trees data frame. 

**d)** Print out a data frame of all the observations *except* for the fourth observation. (i.e. Remove the fourth observation/row.)

```{r}
my.trees[-4,] # (-) Removes and observation 
```
I used a (-) inside my bracket notation to remove row 4. 

**e)** Use the `which()` command to create a vector of row indices that have a `girth` greater than 10. Call that vector `index`.

```{r}
(index <- which(my.trees$Girth > 10)) #which uses a logical and then tells you position of where the logical = TRUE
```
I used which() to know which rows have a girth > 10. 

**f)** Use the `index` vector to create a small data set with just the large girth trees.

```{r}
lg_index <- data.frame(
  Girth = my.trees$Girth[index],
  Height = my.trees$Height[index],
  Volume = my.trees$Volume[index]
)
#sqaure brackets are applying the index logical (??)
```

I created a datafram, lg_index by creating the same column names as before and calling them from the my trees dataset and then  used bracket notation with my index vector to call the rows I was looking for. 

**g)** Use the `index` vector to create a small data set with just the small girth trees.

```{r}
sm_index <- data.frame(
  Girth = my.trees$Girth[-index],
  Height = my.trees$Height[-index],
  Volume = my.trees$Volume[-index]
)

# Used sqaure brackets to sort out non-index trees using (-)
```

I used similar logic to f except I did a (-) index to call all of the rows not in the index vector of my.trees dataframe. 

my.trees$Column - calling the vector and then using [] to apply the index

### Exercise 12 {-}

The following code creates a `data.frame` and then has two different methods for removing the rows with `NA` values in the column `Grade`. Explain the difference between the two.

```{r}
df <- data.frame(name= c('Alice','Bob','Charlie','Daniel'),
                 Grade = c(6,8,NA,9))

df[ -which(  is.na(df$Grade) ), ]
df[  which( !is.na(df$Grade) ), ]
```
The first [ ] uses a -which to call and remove NA and the second [] and the second uses an ! before the is.na to call the opposite of is.na.

### Exercise 14 {-}

Create and manipulate a list.

**a)** Create a list named my.test with elements

  + x = c(4,5,6,7,8,9,10)
  + y = c(34,35,41,40,45,47,51)
  + slope = 2.82
  + p.value = 0.000131
  
```{r}
(my.test <- list(
  x = c(4,5,6,7,8,9,10),
  y = c(34,35,41,40,45,47,51),
  slope = 2.82,
  p.value = 0.000131
))
```
I created a list using the list() function. 
  
**b)** Extract the second element in the list.

```{r}
my.test[2]
```
I used bracket notation to extract the second element in my.test list. 

**c)** Extract the element named `p.value` from the list.
```{r}
my.test['p.value']
```
I used bracket notation with the element name 'p.value' from the my.test list.


Overall - can use square brackets to call specific columns and rows in dataframe and lists. Can also apply a logical to a new datafram to create the columns
